newsitem.title: USA: Space shuttle made ready for Friday launch.
newsitem.headline: Space shuttle made ready for Friday launch.

text.p: Launch pad workers on Wednesday installed insulation on a crucial cooling system for the space shuttle Columbia, fixing a problem which has postponed the craft's launch until Friday.

The shuttle's liftoff, originally set for Thursday, was delayed until 2 p.m. EST/1900 GMT on Friday because of the last-minute discovery that insulating blankets were missing from four coolant pipes in the shuttle's cargo bay.
Engineers feared the exposed pipes, which carry water for cooling the shuttle's electronics, could freeze and burst when they were exposed to the cold vacuum of space.
The loss of one of the spaceship's two cooling systems would force an early return to Earth, Bob Sieck, director of shuttle operations, said.
NASA officials were struggling to explain why the insulation may have been missing from Columbia and possibly its three sister ships for more than 13 years.
"Were these blankets left off intentionally or were they an 'I forgot'? That's what we don't know," Sieck said.

Engineers were digging through a mass of paperwork to find the answers. A quick look at the records indicated that the blankets were fitted for Columbia's first five missions in 1981 and 1982, but may have been removed before a November 1983 flight.

Although the shuttle has flown without the blankets many times and encountered no serious problems, mission managers decided to install the blankets "because it was the prudent thing to do," Sieck said.
The weather outlook for Friday's launch looked promising. U.S. Air Force forecasters gave the shuttle a 90 percent chance of fair weather for launch.
Columbia was to spend 16 days in orbit while a crew of seven astronauts conduct microgravity experiments in a space laboratory.
